newsitem.title: INDIA: India anti-pollution drive clamps down on vehicles.
newsitem.headline: India anti-pollution drive clamps down on vehicles.

text.p: A sweeping anti-pollution campaign in New Delhi has forced more than 200,000 motorists to get their vehicles checked but reduced the toxic content in the capital's air only slightly, officials said on Friday.

The New Delhi government has set an April 15 deadline for vehicles in the capital to get a pollution-check certificate. Cars, scooters and trucks without a sticker will not be allowed to buy petrol after that date.
More than 200,000 owners of cars and scooters visited 218 pollution control stations across the city this week to get the certificate, a Delhi transport ministry official said.
The government had first set a March 19 deadline for pollution checks but extended it after checking centres struggled to deal with the onslaught of vehicles.
"I think it's sheer madness to wait for more than three hours for a certificate," a motorist at the end of a serpentine queue at a checking centre told Reuters.

Central Pollution Control Board chairman Dilip Biswas said atmospheric carbon monoxide had dropped slightly. "At least the trends are encouraging," he said. The Indian capital is the world's fourth most polluted city. About three fourths of its atmospheric pollution is caused by vehicular emissions -- some 900 tonnes a day, or one third of the amount in India's 12 largest cities put together.
New Delhi traffic police booked more than 1,300 offenders for driving without the certificate over the past week before the deadline was extended, the Transport Ministry official said.
But scientists and environmental activists said the drive was aimed at the wrong targets.

"I think what we need is a series of steps like better quality fuel, upgradation of technology at oil refineries, better public transport management and better roads," said Shifali Verma, a scientist at the independent Centre for Science and Environment (CSE).
"If they improve the quality of the fuel, then all the vehicles will automatically start polluting less," Verma said.
About 7,500 people died prematurely in 1996 due to pollution-related diseases in New Delhi, and some 2.5 million people were treated for such illnesses, studies show.

New Delhi, with nearly 11 million residents, is the only major city in the world with buses as its sole means of public transport. A small and infrequent suburban train service offers poor back-up. The city accounts for nearly 10 percent of India's automobiles.

CSE analysts Anju Sharma said the government should introduce stringent measures to ensure manufacturers complied with international emission standards at the manufacturing stage and fitted vehicles with emission-controlling devices.

In 1995, India made it mandatory for new cars to use lead-free fuel and ordered car makers to fit vehicles with catalytic converters to neutralise harmful emissions. But most vehicles are old and do not have emission-control devices.
But environmentalist Iqbal Malik said checking pollution levels was not the solution to New Delhi's problems.

"Their total drive is in the wrong direction. They actually need to concentrate on bringing down the sulphur level in the fuel or do something about the buses that have diesel convertors or the auto rickshaws not running on propane," Malik said.
